name: Margarita
history: The most popular tequila cocktail in the United States. Its exact origin is disputed, with claims spanning 1930s–40s Mexico and the Texas border; the name means "daisy" in Spanish. It is a defining drink of Tex-Mex bars, especially along the border near El Paso.

name: Paloma
history: Mexico's most popular tequila cocktail — far more common there than the margarita. It is traditionally built with grapefruit soda such as Squirt or Jarritos. "Paloma" means "dove" in Spanish.

name: Paloma Sunrise
garnish: Grapefruit or orange slice, lime wheel
history: A modern crossover of two tequila classics — Mexico's Paloma and California's Tequila Sunrise. The Paloma has anchored Mexican cantinas since the mid-20th century, while the Sunrise rose to fame on the Rolling Stones' 1972 tour; this hybrid is a newer, home-bar creation that swaps the Paloma's grapefruit soda for fresh juice and borrows the Sunrise's grenadine glow at the bottom of the glass. The name nods to both parents — the dove and the dawn.

name: Ranch Water
garnish: Lime wedge (Topo Chico, El Paso style)
history: A West Texas highball of tequila, lime, and Topo Chico mineral water. It was born in the Trans-Pecos region around Fort Davis and Marfa and is beloved across far West Texas, including El Paso.

name: Tequila Sunrise
history: Named for the layered colors that form as grenadine settles to the bottom. The modern version was created in the early 1970s in Sausalito, California, and spread widely after the Rolling Stones adopted it on their 1972 tour.

name: Tequila Soda
history: A simple, light highball of tequila and soda water with a squeeze of lime. It has become a modern bar standard for drinkers wanting something crisp and low in sugar.

name: Mexican Mule
history: A tequila twist on the Moscow Mule, swapping vodka for tequila alongside ginger beer and lime. It is sometimes called a "Burro" and is a natural fit anywhere mules and margaritas meet.

name: Vodka Cranberry
history: Also known as the Cape Codder, named for Cape Cod's cranberry bogs. It was popularized by Ocean Spray in the mid-20th century, originally marketed as the "Red Devil."

name: Screwdriver
history: Vodka and orange juice, said to be named by American oil workers in the Persian Gulf who stirred the drink with their screwdrivers. It has been a brunch and bar staple since the 1950s.

name: Vodka Soda
history: The quintessential minimalist highball — just vodka, soda water, and a squeeze of lime. It is a perennial go-to for a clean, low-sugar drink.

name: Vodka Tonic
history: A lighter cousin of the gin and tonic. The quinine in tonic water gives it a crisp, faintly bitter edge that pairs cleanly with vodka.

name: Cosmopolitan
history: A pink vodka cocktail that surged in popularity through the 1990s and was cemented in pop culture by "Sex and the City." It balances vodka and triple sec with cranberry and lime.

name: Sea Breeze
history: A vodka highball with cranberry and grapefruit juice that became a hit in the 1980s. It is tart, refreshing, and named for breezy summer days by the water.

name: Bay Breeze
history: A close relative of the Sea Breeze that swaps grapefruit for pineapple juice, giving it a softer, sweeter tropical profile.

name: Greyhound
history: Vodka and grapefruit juice, dating to the 1930s. Add a salted rim and it becomes its close cousin, the Salty Dog.

name: Madras
history: Vodka with cranberry and orange juice, named after the colorful madras plaid fabric for its reddish-orange hue.

name: Moscow Mule
history: Vodka, ginger beer, and lime, traditionally served in a copper mug. It was invented in 1941 in Los Angeles as a clever way to sell both vodka and ginger beer.

name: Gin and Tonic
history: Born in British colonial India, where tonic's quinine helped fight malaria and gin made the medicine palatable. It has since become a global classic.

name: Tom Collins
history: A tall, fizzy mix of gin, lemon, sugar, and soda. Its name traces to an 1874 New York hoax about a fictitious gossip named Tom Collins.

name: Gin Rickey
history: A dry, unsweetened highball of gin, lime, and soda. It was created in 1880s Washington, D.C., and became a favorite of the Jazz Age.

name: Cuba Libre
history: Rum and cola with lime, born in Cuba around 1900 after Coca-Cola arrived on the island. The name means "Free Cuba," a toast dating to the Spanish-American War era.

name: Daiquiri
history: Rum, lime, and sugar, named for a beach near Santiago de Cuba. A favorite of Ernest Hemingway, it serves as the template for countless variations.

name: Pina Colada
history: Puerto Rico's national drink, blending rum, pineapple, and coconut cream. It was invented in San Juan in the 1950s–60s; the name means "strained pineapple."

name: Dark and Stormy
history: Dark rum floated over ginger beer, originating in Bermuda. Gosling's holds a trademark on the name, made with their Black Seal rum.

name: Whiskey and Coke
history: A straightforward highball pairing whiskey with cola. Ubiquitous in American bars, its most famous form is the "Jack and Coke."

name: Whiskey Sour
history: Whiskey, lemon, and sugar, documented since the 1860s. It is a timeless template — balanced, tart, and easy to love.

name: Whiskey and Ginger
history: Whiskey lengthened with ginger ale, often called a "Jack and Ginger." It is crisp, easygoing, and endlessly popular.

name: Long Island Iced Tea
history: A potent mix of five spirits with a splash of cola that mimics the look of iced tea. Most accounts credit a bartender on Long Island, New York, in the 1970s.

name: Shirley Temple
history: A non-alcoholic favorite of lemon-lime soda and grenadine, finished with a cherry. It was named for the child film star in the 1930s.

name: Roy Rogers
history: The cola-based, non-alcoholic counterpart to the Shirley Temple, named for the singing cowboy actor Roy Rogers.

name: Michelada
garnish: Tajin/salt rim, lime; top with a Mexican lager
history: A Mexican beer cocktail: a cold lager built over lime, hot sauce, and savory seasonings, often with Clamato in the border and Tex-Mex style. It is a beloved hangover cure across Mexico and El Paso. The machine pours the savory mix — top it with beer by hand.

name: Tokyo Tea
history: A Long Island variant that swaps the cola float for Midori, turning the glass a bright radioactive green. It belongs to the family of overbuilt 1970s–80s American bar drinks that stack the whole well into one tall glass. Top it with Sprite by hand.

name: Adios Mfer
history: The blue sibling of the Tokyo Tea — same five-spirit Long Island frame, with blue curacao standing in for the orange liqueur and the cola. Usually shortened to AMF on bar menus, for reasons the full name makes obvious. Top it with Sprite by hand.

name: Midori Sour
history: The drink that made Midori famous in the United States after Suntory launched the melon liqueur stateside in the late 1970s. Sweet, tart, and unmistakably green — a gateway cocktail for anyone who claims not to like liquor.

name: Blue Lagoon
history: A vodka-and-blue-curacao highball usually credited to Andy MacElhone at Harry's New York Bar in Paris. Its whole appeal is the color: a tropical-pool blue that photographs better than it has any right to.

name: Blue Margarita
history: A standard margarita with blue curacao in place of triple sec — both are orange liqueurs, so the flavor barely moves while the color changes completely. A fixture of American Tex-Mex restaurants since the 1970s.

name: Blue Kamikaze
history: The Kamikaze — vodka, orange liqueur, lime — recolored with blue curacao. The original was an American bar drink of the 1970s that spent most of the 1980s and 90s being served as a shot.

name: Green Iguana
history: A melon margarita by another name: tequila and Midori over sour mix. A Tex-Mex bar staple, poured either on the rocks or blended into a frozen.

name: Green Demon
history: A party punch in a glass — vodka and rum hidden under melon liqueur and sour mix. It drinks far easier than it pours, which is the entire trap. Top it with Sprite by hand.

name: Illusion
history: Melon and orange liqueur over vodka, landing somewhere between green and teal depending on the pour. Named for the color, which never quite settles on one.

name: Japanese Slipper
history: Created in Melbourne in the mid-1980s by Jean-Paul Bourguignon at Mietta's restaurant, and one of the few cocktails to come out of Australia and stick. Traditionally equal parts melon liqueur, orange liqueur, and lemon juice.

name: Blue Shark
history: Vodka and tequila in the same glass with blue curacao doing all the talking. Short, cold, and considerably stronger than the color suggests.

name: Tequila Sour
history: The sour template — spirit, citrus, sugar — applied to tequila. It is the margarita's plainer ancestor: drop the orange liqueur and you are left with this.

name: Vodka Sour
history: The most neutral member of the sour family, which is exactly why it gets ordered — all citrus and sugar, with the spirit staying out of the way.

name: Gin Sour
history: One of the oldest sours on record, predating the whiskey sour's American popularity. Add soda water and you have a Tom Collins.

name: Rum Sour
history: Effectively a daiquiri built on sour mix instead of fresh lime and sugar — the same drink the Caribbean has been making since the 1890s, taken the quick way.

name: Gin Gimlet
history: Gin and lime, traditionally with lime cordial. The often-repeated story ties it to British sailors taking lime against scurvy; the link is popular but not well documented.

name: Tequila Shot
history: Straight pour, no ceremony required — though the salt-and-lime ritual is an American addition, not a Mexican one. In Mexico, good tequila is usually sipped.

name: Vodka Shot
history: The plainest thing the machine can do. Traditionally served near-freezing across Eastern Europe and Russia, and traditionally accompanied by food.

name: Gin Shot
history: Rarely ordered, occasionally deserved. Gin is juniper-forward by definition, so a straight pour tastes like a very small forest.

name: White Rum Shot
history: Light rum, filtered and aged briefly, is built for mixing — which makes taking it neat a statement of some kind.

name: Midori Shot
history: Suntory's melon liqueur, launched in the United States in 1978 at a Studio 54 party. Sweet enough to count as dessert and green enough to see from across the room.

name: Blue Kamikaze Shot
history: The shot form of the Blue Kamikaze, and the way it is most often served. Bright blue, sharply tart, and gone in one motion.

name: Melon Ball Shot
history: Named for the scooped melon it is meant to taste like. Normally built with pineapple or orange juice; on sour mix it comes out sharper and considerably greener.
